title: Architectural Lessons From Environmental Psychology: The Case of Biophilic Architecture
review_question: To review findings from environmental psychology and aesthetics to argue for the integration of natural contents and structural landscape features in the built environment (biophilic architecture) to positively influence human psychological and physiological well-being.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Not explicitly specified; draws on empirical findings from diverse psychological subdisciplines.

findings.antecedent: Environments (natural vs. urban)
findings.source: The Psychoevolutionary Framework
findings.quote: empirical evidence shows that environments (e.g., urban vs. natural) are processed according to their affective valence.

findings.antecedent: Landscape qualities (prospect, refuge)
findings.source: Aesthetic Preference and Structural Landscape Features
findings.quote: human beings' preference for landscapes correlates with two environmental qualities: prospect and refuge.

findings.antecedent: Visual cues (complexity, gross structural properties/patterns, depth properties, ground surface/texture, absence of threats, deflected vista)
findings.source: Aesthetic Preference and Structural Landscape Features
findings.quote: Ulrich's psychoevolutionary framework lists some other visual cues that are associated with immediate positive affective reactions

findings.antecedent: Structural landscape properties (complexity, mystery, coherence, legibility)
findings.consequent: Positive aesthetic evaluations, positive influence on landscape selections
findings.source: Aesthetic Preference and Structural Landscape Features
findings.quote: each of which correlates with positive aesthetic evaluations and positively influences landscape selections.

findings.antecedent: Natural, vegetated landscapes
findings.source: The Aesthetic Appeal of Natural Contents
findings.quote: individuals consistently prefer natural, vegetated landscapes over urban settings without vegetation.

findings.antecedent: Urban settings containing some vegetation (especially trees) or a water feature
findings.source: The Aesthetic Appeal of Natural Contents
findings.quote: highest preference is associated with urban settings containing some vegetation, especially trees, or a water feature

findings.antecedent: Nonnatural environments (home and working interiors)
findings.consequent: Presence of actual vegetative elements or decorative references to natural content
findings.source: The Aesthetic Appeal of Natural Contents
findings.quote: nonnatural environments (e.g., home and working interiors) often contain actual vegetative elements or (decorative) references to natural content

findings.antecedent: Flowers
findings.source: The Aesthetic Appeal of Natural Contents
findings.quote: some studies show that these elements are indeed associated with positive aesthetic reactions

findings.antecedent: Savanna-type landscapes
findings.source: The Savanna Hypothesis
findings.quote: Balling and Falk (1982) found that young individuals preferred savannas over other biomes without ever being exposed to the former type of landscape.

findings.antecedent: Tree shapes characteristic of high-quality savannas (low trunk, broad canopy, moderate canopy layering)
findings.source: The Savanna Hypothesis
findings.quote: research indicates that people tend to prefer tree shapes characteristic of high-quality savannas

findings.antecedent: Natural settings
findings.source: Naturalness and Stress Reduction
findings.quote: Natural settings have been found to be ideally suited to restore or rest directed attention

findings.antecedent: Natural unthreatening (savanna-like) settings, open/low-risk environments, calm water features, small fire, availability of resources
findings.source: Naturalness and Stress Reduction
findings.quote: restorative responses typically occurred in natural unthreatening (savanna-like) settings.

findings.antecedent: Hospital rooms with views of a small tree group (vs. brown brick wall)
findings.consequent: Hospital stays, negative comments from nurses, analgesics, postoperative complications
findings.source: Naturalness and Stress Reduction
findings.quote: patients with the tree view had shorter hospital stays, received fewer negative comments from the nurses, required less moderate and strong analgesics, and had slightly fewer postoperative complications.

findings.antecedent: Natural objects
findings.source: The Value of Nature-Based, or Biophilic, Architecture
findings.quote: humans have a (partly) hardwired emotional affiliation with certain classes of natural objects.

findings.antecedent: Reduced contact with nature
findings.consequent: Reduced knowledge of natural forms, impoverished conceptual framework for natural objects
findings.source: The Value of Nature-Based, or Biophilic, Architecture
findings.quote: reduced contact with nature can be accompanied by a reduced knowledge of the rich variety of forms characteristic of natural entities.

findings.antecedent: Integrating naturalistic elements in architecture
findings.consequent: Dominance of functional semantic networks and associated epistemological attitude
findings.source: The Value of Nature-Based, or Biophilic, Architecture
findings.quote: integrating naturalistic elements in architecture can counteract the increasing dominance of functional semantic networks and the associated epistemological attitude.

findings.antecedent: Biophilic design
findings.consequent: Attentiveness to object's perceptual qualities, attention to functions/functionalist postures
findings.source: The Value of Nature-Based, or Biophilic, Architecture
findings.quote: Biophilic design could lead to more attentiveness to an object's perceptual qualities, thereby leading attention away from its possible functions and the associated functionalist postures.

findings.antecedent: Nature-based architecture
findings.consequent: Fascination for natural forms, proenvironmental behavior
findings.source: The Value of Nature-Based, or Biophilic, Architecture
findings.quote: nature-based architecture can awaken fascination for natural forms. Such an attitude could be ecologically relevant, because it is found that proenvironmental behavior is positively influenced by emotional states toward nature

findings.antecedent: Uniform (modernist) environments
findings.source: The Value of Nature-Based, or Biophilic, Architecture
findings.quote: an increasing dominance of uniform (modernist) environments will probably have a number of psychological and physiological costs.

findings.antecedent: Environments lacking natural content/structure (modern urban settings)
findings.consequent: Negatively toned feelings, stress-related endocrinal reactions
findings.source: The Value of Nature-Based, or Biophilic, Architecture
findings.quote: Exposure to such environments could rapidly and automatically trigger negatively toned feelings and the associated stress-related endocrinal reactions

findings.antecedent: Specific architectural interventions (e.g., reducing lighting, lowering ceilings, small windowless spaces for refuge; larger space, raised ceilings, thin transparent walls, wide views for prospect)
findings.source: Integrating Structural Landscape Features in Architecture
findings.quote: feelings of prospect and refuge can be evoked by specific architectural interventions.

findings.antecedent: Balanced presence of complexity and coherence in built settings
findings.source: Integrating Structural Landscape Features in Architecture
findings.quote: a balanced presence of both properties contributes to the aesthetic qualities of built settings

findings.antecedent: Deflected vista (e.g., bending corridor)
findings.source: Integrating Structural Landscape Features in Architecture
findings.quote: The most straightforward way to apply mystery to an architectural setting is by deflected vista.

findings.antecedent: Indirect experiences of nature (vegetation, nature pictures, screensavers)
findings.source: Integrating Natural Contents in Architecture
findings.quote: integrating vegetation in built settings, by hanging nature pictures on the wall, by nature-oriented screensavers, and so on... are what Stephen Kellert (2005) called indirect experiences of nature

findings.antecedent: Incorporation of trees and tree forms (actual or symbolic) in built environment
findings.source: Integrating Natural Contents in Architecture
findings.quote: The incorporation of trees and tree forms, actual or symbolic, into the built environment should have a strong positive impact on people.

findings.antecedent: Architectural elements on different dimensions (e.g., color, form, movement)
findings.source: Integrating Natural Contents in Architecture
findings.quote: architectural elements on different dimensions of their artistic work... can make an important contribution to the overall aesthetic experience.

findings.antecedent: Fractal characteristics (of natural scenes/vegetation)
findings.source: Applying Nature's Fractal Geometry to Architecture
findings.quote: fractal characteristics could as well be associated with biophilic responses to typical natural contents, such as vegetation?

findings.antecedent: Fractal patterns
findings.consequent: Associations of naturalness in human subjects
findings.source: Applying Nature's Fractal Geometry to Architecture
findings.quote: fractal patterns evoke associations of naturalness in human subjects

findings.antecedent: Contact with fractals
findings.consequent: Ability to perceptually differentiate between highly similar natural patterns
findings.source: Applying Nature's Fractal Geometry to Architecture
findings.quote: contact with fractals improves the ability to perceptually differentiate between highly similar natural patterns

findings.antecedent: Fractal patterns (vs. nonfractals)
findings.source: Applying Nature's Fractal Geometry to Architecture
findings.quote: more than 90% of a group of 120 students preferred fractal patterns over nonfractals.

findings.antecedent: Fractal patterns with fractal dimension between 1.17 and 1.38 (average 1.26 ± 0.06)
findings.source: Applying Nature's Fractal Geometry to Architecture
findings.quote: 24 study participants preferred fractal patterns with a fractal dimension of between 1.17 and 1.38.

findings.antecedent: Fractal patterns with fractal dimension between 1.3 and 1.5 (vs. 1.1-1.2 and 1.6-1.9)
findings.source: Applying Nature's Fractal Geometry to Architecture
findings.quote: patterns with a fractal dimension of between 1.3 and 1.5 were preferred most

findings.antecedent: Fractal patterns with midrange fractal dimension (1.4 to 1.6, mean 1.54)
findings.source: Applying Nature's Fractal Geometry to Architecture
findings.quote: attractors with a fractal dimension ranging from 1.4 to 1.6 (mean fractal dimension of 1.54) received the highest preference ratings.

findings.antecedent: Fractal patterns with fractal dimension ranging from 1.2 to 1.4
findings.consequent: Ability to recognize and find new shapes
findings.source: Applying Nature's Fractal Geometry to Architecture
findings.quote: recognizing and finding new shapes in fractal patterns is best for those patterns with a fractal dimension ranging from 1.2 to 1.4.

findings.antecedent: Fractal patterns with dimension values greater than 1.3
findings.source: Applying Nature's Fractal Geometry to Architecture
findings.quote: the variance in study participants' judgments of the complexity of fractal patterns exploded when pictures had dimension values greater than 1.3.

findings.antecedent: Forest photograph, savanna representation (vs. control picture)
findings.source: Applying Nature's Fractal Geometry to Architecture
findings.quote: the change in conductance between work and rest periods was 3% lower for the forest photograph and 44% lower for the savanna representation than for the control picture.

findings.antecedent: Savanna picture with fractal dimension 1.3-1.5
findings.source: Applying Nature's Fractal Geometry to Architecture
findings.quote: the pattern that was most effective in stress reduction, the savanna picture, had a fractal dimension that fell within the range of dimension values that was earlier found to correlate with highest aesthetic preference

findings.antecedent: Fractal dimension of nature scene silhouettes
findings.source: Applying Nature's Fractal Geometry to Architecture
findings.quote: a modest but significant correlation between mean preference and the fractal dimension of the silhouettes.

synthesis_conclusions: Humans possess a hardwired emotional affiliation with natural elements and landscapes, stemming from evolutionary history.
Contact with nature, or nature-based forms in architecture, positively influences psychological and physiological functioning, including stress reduction and attention restoration.
Modern urban environments often lack natural features and structural organization, potentially leading to psychological and physiological costs and negative affective states.

Biophilic architecture, by integrating natural contents (e.g., vegetation, water) and structural landscape features (e.g., prospect-refuge, complexity, coherence, mystery, fractal geometry), can mitigate these adverse effects.
Fractal geometry, particularly patterns with an intermediate fractal dimension (around 1.3-1.5), is a key characteristic of naturalness that contributes to aesthetic preference and stress reduction.
Architectural interventions can effectively evoke feelings of prospect, refuge, complexity, coherence, and mystery, which are associated with positive aesthetic and restorative outcomes.
evidence_gaps: Lack of comparative research between natural settings and architecturally rich buildings that emulate natural geometry.
Need for a broader account of genetic predispositions to inhabited landscapes beyond the savanna hypothesis.
Unclear relation between abstract structural landscape features and preference for water elements.
Lack of clarity on how the genetic component of positive affiliations with nature should be understood.
Need for further research on the topic of fractal aesthetics and its relations to biophilia.
Unclear whether naturalness or complexity is the primary underlying cause of biophilic responses to fractals.
Unclear whether fractal dimension or specific depicted contents primarily underlie restorative responses in natural scenes.
Question of whether aesthetic tastes for nature-based forms are held by the general public or primarily by artists, and if changes in taste are broadly appreciated.
The preliminary nature of some experimental outcomes (e.g., fractal dimension and stress reduction) necessitates replication.
The explanation of biophilic responses to fractals in terms of noise signals emitted by the nervous system is on a different level than the evolutionary account, and their connection is unclear.
limitations: The theoretical merits of 'biophilia' have been questioned, though the term is used synthetically in the paper.
Some natural features can cause negative or aversive reactions in humans, not exclusively positive ones.
Experimental outcomes are sometimes difficult to integrate into a coherent, overarching conceptual framework.
Differences in nature appreciation are often not fully explored in discussions.
Reduced contact with nature may lead to an impoverished conceptual framework and reduced knowledge of natural forms.
The increasing dominance of uniform (modernist) environments may have psychological and physiological costs.
Not all architecture throughout history contains references to natural form, suggesting that tastes are not exclusively dictated by biological predispositions.
Much architecture does not display the profound fractality of Hindu or Gothic architecture, potentially casting doubt on a hypothesized universal preference for fractal-like patterns.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Natural environments and biophilic architectural elements facilitate the restoration of directed attention, reducing mental fatigue and improving cognitive function.
Exposure to natural environments and biophilic architectural elements can reduce physiological stress indicators (e.g., heart rate, blood pressure) and promote positive emotional states.
Humans possess an innate, genetically determined tendency to affiliate with nature and other living systems, which biophilic architecture aims to satisfy for human well-being.

mechanism_chain.description: Biophilic architectural elements trigger physiological and cognitive responses that mediate the connection between the environment and human well-being, including affective valence.

steps.from_construct: exposure to natural elements (e.g., views of nature, natural light)
steps.to_construct: reduced physiological arousal (e.g., lower heart rate, cortisol levels)
improved cognitive performance and reduced mental fatigue

stimulus_images.description: Photographic examples of biophilic design elements and principles applied in various architectural settings.
Diagram illustrating the conceptual framework linking biophilic design to human psychological and physiological outcomes.

environmental_features: views of nature (e.g., vegetation, water bodies)
natural materials (e.g., wood, stone, natural fibers)
biomorphic forms and patterns (e.g., fractals, organic shapes)
urban environments (e.g., concrete, artificial light, lack of natural elements)
